artwork.title: Liberty Leading the People
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Shonagon, 2024, after the restoration, via Wikimedia Commons · Public Domain

lessons.title: An idea with bare feet

n1.text: Smoke, a barricade, and a woman with a flag stepping over the dead, a crowd surging behind her. The canvas is over three metres wide. Delacroix painted it in about four months, September to December 1830.

q1.text: Where does your eye go first?

b1a.text: The flag tops a triangle: Liberty's raised arm and the flagpole form its peak, the barricade its base. Guns, arms and the pole cut across it in diagonals: order and momentum at once.

b1b.text: That's where you stand: at the barricade's edge. Two dead soldiers and a half-dressed man lie almost at your feet. Delacroix drew this foreground of the dead from Gros and from Géricault's Raft of the Medusa.

b1c.text: A schoolboy turned fighter, a pistol in each hand and a Royal Guard cartridge pouch. The Louvre says he inspired Gavroche, the street boy in Victor Hugo's Les Misérables.

n2.text: Every route leads upward: from the dead, through the crowd, to the flag. And the canvas splits on a diagonal: a dark lower half, and a lit upper half where Liberty stands haloed against the light.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: Feel the rush, then look at the order: the dead, the crowd, the flag. Every line climbs toward the light.

b2a.text: That's everyone's first guess, but no: this is a later revolution.

correction.tempting: Liberty, the tricolour and the Phrygian cap all look like 1789, the Revolution everyone learns about at school.
correction.truth: This is July 1830: three days of street fighting, 27 to 29 July, that drove out King Charles X.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's full title is "The 28th of July 1830. Liberty Leading the People", and the canvas is signed and dated in red paint, on the right: "Eug. Delacroix. 1830".

b2b.text: Right. In July 1830, Paris fought for three days and drove out Charles X. The Louvre's full title even names the day: "The 28th of July 1830".

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: July 1830, not 1789. I began the canvas that September and signed it that same year.

b2c.text: Close in spirit, but no. Paris rose again in 1848; this painting shows the uprising before it.

correction.tempting: 1848 was another Paris revolution, and this very painting is tied up with that year: it came out of hiding then.
correction.truth: It shows July 1830 and was painted that autumn, eighteen years before 1848.
correction.evidence: It's signed "Eug. Delacroix. 1830". In March 1848, after the new revolution, the state reclaimed it from Delacroix, who had kept it at relatives' since about 1839.

n3.text: July 1830. Charles X issued ordinances against the spirit of the 1814 Charter; Paris fought for three days, the "Three Glorious Days". He abdicated, and Louis-Philippe became "king of the French".

n3b.text: That's why the flag matters. The restored Bourbon kings flew plain royal white. In July 1830 the blue-white-red tricolour came back on the barricades. Look far right, through the smoke: another one flies on Notre-Dame's towers.

q3.text: Is the woman with the flag a real fighter?

choices.label: Yes, a real woman from that day

b3a.text: Not quite, though it's easy to see why she feels real. She's something else.

correction.tempting: Everyone around her is a recognisable Parisian type in real clothes with real weapons, and she carries a real musket with a bayonet.
correction.truth: She's an allegory: an abstract idea, Liberty, given a human body and recognised by her attributes.
correction.evidence: Her attributes give her away: the Phrygian cap, an ancient sign of freedom, and the tricolour. Her bare breast and perfect Greek profile come from ancient art, not from the street.

b3b.text: Right. She's Liberty, an idea given a body: an allegory. You know her by the Phrygian cap, an ancient sign of freedom, and the tricolour.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: Don't look for her name. She is Liberty herself: the Phrygian cap, the tricolour, bare feet on the rubble.

n4.text: That's the shock of the picture: an ancient ideal, bare-breasted with a Greek profile, walking barefoot through a modern street fight. Delacroix had already tried out this antique woman in Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi, in 1826.

n4b.text: He changed his mind about her, too. X-rays show her face was first painted from the front, then turned into a perfect profile. A change the artist makes while painting is called a repentir.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: I first set her face towards you, then turned it into profile. A painter's second thought.

q4.text: Top hat, waistcoat, hunting gun. Who does the Louvre say he is?

b4a.text: That's not how the Louvre reads him, though the top hat makes it a natural guess.

correction.tempting: To us a top hat means a gentleman, and he looks smarter than the man in the beret beside him.
correction.truth: The Louvre's teaching dossier reads him as a journeyman, craftsman or workshop foreman, carrying a double-barrelled shotgun. Readings of the crowd's classes do vary.
correction.evidence: Look at his red flannel belt, beside the factory worker with a sabre and the kneeling labourer: the dossier reads them as different kinds of working Paris, side by side.

b4b.text: Right. The Louvre's teaching dossier reads him as a journeyman, craftsman or workshop foreman, with a double-barrelled shotgun and a red flannel belt.

n5.text: Factory worker, craftsman, countryside labourer, schoolboy: Delacroix packs Paris into one surge behind an idea. As Smarthistory puts it, he would have us believe everyone can be a revolutionary. And Delacroix himself?

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: I have undertaken a modern subject, a barricade, and although I may not have fought for my country, at least I shall have painted for her.
voice.cite: Letter to his brother Charles, 28 October 1830 (English translation: Smarthistory)

n5b.text: Now look at how he paints. The palette is mostly coloured greys. Blue, white and red flicker in small touches all over the canvas, so the whole picture rhymes with the flag. He leaves out green, orange and violet.

q5.text: Since 2024, Liberty's dress looks different. Did restorers repaint it?

b5a.text: No, it's the opposite. The restorers took paint away; they didn't add a new design.

correction.tempting: After cleaning, her dress went from solid yellow to grey and gold, a change big enough to look like a redesign.
correction.truth: Restorers thinned yellowed varnish and removed retouching from 1949. What reappeared is Delacroix's own paint.
correction.evidence: The 1949 repaints were very soluble and sat on top. Underneath: Delacroix's grey dress, with yellow laid on densely at the bodice and thinning toward her legs.

b5b.text: Exactly. Orange retouching from 1949 had made the dress read as solid yellow. Underneath: a grey dress with yellow dense at the bodice, thinning toward the legs, as Delacroix left it.

n6.text: The cleaning brought back more: a worn shoe at bottom left, lost in the varnish, and the cool overall colour. The Louvre's curator Côme Fabre said the aim was to do justice to the work of "a colourist of genius".

n6b.text: No king ordered this painting. Delacroix made it on his own and showed it at the 1831 Salon, to mixed reviews. The state bought it for 3,000 francs, then took it down, fearing it would encourage riots.

n6c.text: Stored, handed back to Delacroix around 1839, reclaimed in 1848, it reached the Louvre only in 1874. One more link: Delacroix had posed for Géricault's Raft of the Medusa, face down among the dying.

voice.speaker: delacroix
voice.text: I posed for Géricault's raft, face down among the dying. You'll meet that painting next.

lessons.takeaway: July 1830, not 1789: an ancient allegory walks into a modern street fight, built on a pyramid and coloured like the flag.
